what_this_is: The Workshop row for the tool in tools/export-records-as-list-rows: turning a person's records on disk (JSON, tab-separated files, markdown tables) into the payloads that put rows into their Trillion lists, by a mapping file the person writes. A script the person's AI runs on the person's own computer.

payload.label: Turn my records into rows for my Trillion lists (runs on your computer)
payload.job: Take records I keep in files (JSON, spreadsheets saved as tab-separated text, markdown tables) and prepare them as rows for my lists, using a mapping I write once
payload.description: Reads a mapping file the person gives: the lists to make and, for each source of records, where the records are, which to drop, what to work out from each and how a row is made from it (fields copied, filled into templates, read as numbers or dates, mapped to a list's choices, joined, counted in a file). Writes make_lists.json, the rows in batches and a manifest into a folder the person names. It sends nothing: the batches are put into the lists afterwards. Row ids are stable, so loading the same rows twice updates them. Rows whose ids are in a skip file are left out, so existing rows are never overwritten. When two records make the same row id the mapping must say which one to keep, because choosing silently would drop a record. A re-run replaces only the files an earlier run wrote. It knows no record kinds: every file, column and list comes from the mapping.

mapping.description: The mapping file on the person's computer (the README describes its keys), put where {mapping} is in the command.

root.description: The folder the mapping's files and globs are relative to, put where {root} is in the command.

out.description: The folder to write the payloads into, put where {out} is in the command.

output_schema.description: The last JSON the script prints: { <source name>: { list_id, rows } }, the number of rows each source made. The payloads and manifest.json are in the folder; exit status 2 with a reason on standard error when the mapping or a file could not be read.

invoke.say: This runs on the person's own computer, never on Trillion. If they have no mapping yet, write one with them from the README: look at a few of their records, name each list's fields, and say for each source where its records are and how each field is made. Run `run`, read the counts and the manifest in the output folder, and tell the person how many rows each source made. A refusal says what to change, for example which source makes two rows with one id. The script sends nothing; putting the batches into the lists is a separate step they approve. Use `--only SOURCE` to run one source, `--batch N` for the batch size and `--skip-ids FILE` to leave out rows already in the lists.

provenance.source: Written for the Workshop: a declarative record-to-row mapping, in the way a data-loading tool maps source columns to a target table

payload.label: Prepare records for my lists with their sources and basis (runs on your computer)
payload.job: Take records I keep in files and prepare everything to put them into my lists as records, each value with where it came from and how sure we are, in batches I can send
payload.description: Reads the mapping and source files from the one folder the person granted this tool. A declared records source reads only its type and id prefix through this run's scoped records capability; its sender config and Keychain credential are not used. Maps each source by the person's rules, then returns counts, pending or diverted items and the records:write commands as result data. It writes no local file and sends no records. A row with no address, two rows with one id, a link to a row that does not exist, a value over the limit or a basis naming too many sources is refused by name. It knows no record kinds or lists: all of it comes from the mapping.

mapping.description: The mapping file inside the folder granted to this tool.

roots.description: The mapping's other folders as quoted --root NAME=DIR pairs. They must also be inside the granted folder.

source_type.description: The one source record type this run is granted to list; the run right is filled from this field.

source_prefix.description: The source id prefix this run is granted to list; the run right is filled from this field.

provenance.source: Written for the Workshop: a declarative mapping from staged records to write commands, with a basis kept for each derived value

payload.label: Send prepared batches into my lists, resuming where I stopped (runs on your computer)
payload.job: Put the batches of rows I prepared into my lists one at a time, wait and retry when the list is busy, split a batch that is too big, and remember what was already sent
payload.description: Reads a config the person gives (the command that writes rows into a list, optionally a command to wake the list first, the errors that mean wait and retry, the errors that mean the batch is too big, the waits and the order). Sends each batch of an export in order, counts what the command kept, writes progress to a status file and skips what it already sent when run again. A batch counts only when every row was kept; a refusal stops the run and the status file names the batch and the reason.

config.description: The config file, put where {config} is in the command.

batches.description: The folder an export wrote, put where {batches} is in the command.

status.description: The progress file, put where {status} is in the command.

output_schema.description: The status the script prints: { state: all_batches_sent | stopped_on_refusal, batches_done, last_refusal? }. Exit 0 all sent, 1 refused, 2 unreadable.

invoke.say: This runs on the person's own computer and writes into their lists, so run it only when they ask to send. Read the status: how many batches were sent and, if it stopped, which batch and why. A stop can be re-run later; it resumes.

provenance.source: Written for the Workshop: a resumable batch sender with warm-up, retry and halving

payload.label: Publish what a saved view of my list shows into a file my site shows (runs on your computer)
payload.job: Put the rows one saved view of my list shows (a changelog, the articles I marked public) into a file my website renders when it is next deployed, without opening my account to the internet
payload.description: Takes what tool:read-a-list-view read for one saved view (one page holding the whole view: the rows its rules keep, in its order, with the list's fields) and a config naming the view's record id, and writes { schema, source: { view, list, blake3 }, fields, rows: [{ id, values }] }. With media in the config, the pictures and recordings the rows name are copied into the site's own static files under the BLAKE3 of their bytes (never twice) and the rows name the site's address. The BLAKE3 of the fields and rows is the file's key, so publishing the same rows again writes nothing. A read that holds only part of the view publishes nothing. It names no list, view or field.

read.description: The file holding tool:read-a-list-view's answer for the view, put where {read} is in the command.

config.description: The config file (view, and media when the rows' pictures are carried into the site), put where {config} is in the command.

out.description: The file the site renders, put where {out} is in the command.

output_schema.description: What the script prints: { file, rows, of, blake3, media: { copied, kept, not_public }, written }. written is false when the file already held these rows. Exit 0 published or current, 2 unreadable config or read, a read of part of the view, or a missing media file.

get_it: python3 -m pip install -U blake3   # or have the b3sum command
needs: blake3 (the python module) or the b3sum command
invoke.say: This runs on the person's own computer, from the root of the Workshop checkout. Read the view first with tool:read-a-list-view (a limit at least the view's rows) into the read file. This writes one file there; nothing goes online until their site is deployed with it, which needs their yes. Tell them how many rows the view showed of how many, and whether the file changed.

provenance.source: Written for the Workshop: a one-way publish of a saved list view into a site's data file

payload.label: Note new releases or commits from a repository (runs on your computer)
payload.job: Read a person's release mark or commit branch, stage each new entry once with its source identity, and let their mapping make list rows
payload.description: Reads settings the person gives: a program in the repository that prints JSON naming a release, a git ref for the newest release, or a commit branch where each commit is one entry. In commit mode, each entry has the commit identity, date and its own subject; the first run may start after an explicit commit, and skip_subjects are filters in the settings. The staged file is what the person's mapping turns into rows. The sender with keep_held writes only rows the list lacks, so an existing row or a person's edits are preserved. The tool does not infer push boundaries or group commits by day, and knows no product, list or road.

settings.description: The settings file (mark, fields, most_subjects, and optionally each, after and skip_subjects), put where {settings} is in the command.

repository.description: The repository folder, put where {repository} is in the command.

staged.description: The staged file of releases, put where {staged} is in the command.

output_schema.description: What the script prints: { releases, added, added_count }, added being the name of the newest entry added or null. Exit 0, or 2 when the settings, the repository or the mark could not be read.

needs: the mark command's runtime, when the mark is a command
invoke.say: This runs on the person's own computer, from the root of the Workshop checkout, and only reads their repository. Say how many entries were added and the newest entry name. A mark command also needs its own runtime; a git ref does not. Entries are commits, not inferred pushes.

provenance.source: Written for the Workshop: releases and their commit subjects as staged records

payload.label: Put prepared records into my account through my door, writing only what it lacks (runs on your computer)
payload.job: Put the records I prepared into my account so a re-run writes nothing: read what my account holds, send only what differs (or, when I keep edited rows, only what it lacks), in small commands, and stop at the first refusal
payload.description: Takes the result of tool:build-records-to-write directly. Through this run's separately scoped records door, it reads only the target record kinds declared on this row, skips records already held when keep_held is true, or merges source changes against an optional previous-import baseline while preserving live edits and deletions. It reports conflicts, writes bounded commands with fresh per-run request keys, reconciles unknown write outcomes and returns readback counts; a mismatching readback is never all_written. It reads no host payload file, config, keychain item or sender credential. The standalone send_record_write.py command remains available for a person who chooses the manual computer workflow.
The whole result object returned by tool:build-records-to-write, including commands.

target_type.description: The one target record type this run is granted to read and write; the run right is filled from this field.

target_prefix.description: The target record id prefix this run is granted to read and write; the run right is filled from this field.

keep_held.description: When true, leave every target record already held as it is, including rows edited since they were first written.

baseline.description: The previous imported builder payload. Refresh source fields only where the live value still matches this baseline; retain live edits/deletions and report conflicts. Cannot be combined with keep_held.

provenance.source: Written for the Workshop: the records:write sender that writes only what an account lacks
